choices: true, because both hold the text "hi"
false, because they are two separate objects
true, because Java shares all equal strings
It does not compile - == cannot be used on Strings
explanation: new String(...) deliberately makes a fresh object each time, so a and b name two different objects that happen to hold the same characters. == asks whether the two names point at the same object, which they do not. a.equals(b) asks about the characters and is true. Literals are a special case: the compiler shares them, which is why "hi" == "hi" is often true and why this mistake survives so much testing.
hints: == on objects compares identity. Which two objects exist here?
new String(...) is a promise to create a new object rather than reuse one.
